body.x: Cities and expressways with advanced transportation infrastructure already have a large number of CCTV cameras, but most of them remain one-way monitoring tools that control-room operators check with their own eyes. Measuring accurate traffic volume and vehicle types has also meant burying detectors (VDS/AVC) or sending surveyors onto the road, which brings heavy road-surface construction costs, lane closures and on-site safety risks. CITYEYELAB, a deep-tech startup founded in Pangyo in January 2021, overcomes these limits by using AI to analyze footage from CCTV cameras already installed on existing roads.

CITYEYELAB developed CITY.EYE, an AI video analytics solution, based on its vision of "One Platform, Any Video Source, All Mobility Tasks." Conventional video analytics relied on single-image capture and struggled to recognize vehicles that overlap or appear at night or in bad weather. CITYEYELAB instead introduced trajectory-based analysis, which tracks each vehicle from the moment it enters the frame until it leaves. It also applies patented 3D geometric calibration to correct distortion caused by differences in camera height and angle, and derives vehicle position and speed along with detailed 6-class and 12-class vehicle classification.

The technology was proven through the Korea Expressway Corporation's AI-based Traffic Survey and Verification System project. Using footage from about 9,500 CCTV cameras installed on expressways nationwide, CITYEYELAB successfully delivered a system that automatically produces 12-class vehicle classification, traffic volume and speed, and it achieved stable accuracy of 95% or higher across diverse road environments. The system also lets users verify output data by checking it directly against the source footage, which substantially raises data reliability.

CITYEYELAB continues to expand its portfolio with CITY.SIGNAL, a signal optimization simulation solution; CITY.AV, an infrastructure-cooperative dynamic traffic information platform demonstrated at the intersection north of Pangyo Station and with the Panta-G Bus (Pangyo's autonomous shuttle bus); and CITY.SAFE, an early electric vehicle fire detection platform. In B2G, the technology serves road management agencies and local governments for traffic policy and public procurement. In B2B, it is expanding to engineering firms that conduct traffic impact assessments, drive-through and large-building commercial area analysis, system integration (SI) companies for control systems, and CCTV and edge equipment makers.

body.x: For overseas expansion, the company plans to open markets through technology partnerships with local traffic engineering firms and SI companies. Its platform can extract traffic data simply by uploading existing CCTV footage, with no separate road-surface sensors or electromagnetic detector construction. CITYEYELAB is currently seeking Pre-Series A investment. It plans to step up its participation in overseas city-related exhibitions from 2027 and to look for global partners, with the goal of attending CES 2028.

AVING News met with CITYEYELAB CEO Jongwoo Jung in Pangyo Techno Valley to discuss CITY.EYE, the AI traffic survey solution that turns the 9,500 CCTV cameras already installed along Korean expressways into traffic sensors, how CITY.SIGNAL and CITY.AV take video analytics from recognition to action, how the company plans to take its platform overseas through partners, and what Pangyo offers a company like CITYEYELAB.
Q1. Please introduce CITYEYELAB.

A. CITYEYELAB, as the name suggests, is a company that acts as the eyes of the city. Our mission is "One Platform, Any Video Source, All Mobility Tasks." In line with that mission, we connect the CCTV cameras across a city and use their footage to generate a range of traffic information.
Q2. How does your technology use the CCTV cameras that are already installed?

A. A single intersection in a city can have six to seven CCTV cameras, and sometimes as many as 10. Most existing CCTV is used for control: operators in a control center watch the footage. As AI has advanced, we have developed AI video-analytics technology that works with existing control CCTV as it is. Once the footage reaches the control center, AI can run on it there, so there is no need to add AI at the camera site.
Q3. What is your flagship solution, and where has it been applied?

A. Our flagship solution is CITY.EYE, an AI traffic survey solution. Our main deployment is with the Korea Expressway Corporation, where 9,500 CCTV cameras are already installed along Korean expressways. Until now, those cameras have been used mostly for control. People watched the footage to judge whether traffic was congested or flowing, or whether an accident had occurred. With our system, traffic information is generated automatically from the CCTV footage.
Q4. Where do you want to take this next?
A. We want to build a system in which control CCTV automatically recognizes and assesses accidents, safety issues and road conditions such as potholes, and alerts control-room operators in advance.
Q5. What other solutions do you offer beyond traffic surveys?

A. Through video analytics, we keep building mobility systems that go beyond simple recognition to action. CITY.SIGNAL is a signal optimization solution. It generates traffic information from city intersections, simulates how traffic signals should be operated based on that information, and verifies the effect. CITY.AV provides dynamic traffic information for cooperative autonomous driving. We are using it to give the Panta-G Bus (Pangyo's autonomous shuttle bus) infrastructure-level traffic information in the form of a 3D map.
Q6. Who uses your solutions?

A. Our customers fall into private and public sectors. In the private sector, most are engineering firms. When they build a building or widen a road, they have to survey how the traffic environment will change before and after, and that requires traffic information. We produce that traffic information and deliver the data. Drive-through stores are another example. When they or other buildings are planned, the traffic volume and foot traffic around the site have to be analyzed, and our system is used for that as well.

In the public sector, our solutions are used mainly when setting traffic operation policy. Korea conducts a traffic survey every October, and the United States, Europe and other Asian countries conduct one about once a year or about once a month. Our services are used for those surveys.
Q7. Why are you building a platform, and how does it help you expand overseas?

A. We are building a platform because our goal is to export. As I mentioned, public and private organizations abroad also need to collect traffic information in the same way as in Korea. In overseas cases, traffic surveys have mostly relied on electromagnetic sensors installed under the road. With our platform, traffic information can be generated simply by uploading recorded video. So we aim to build the platform and open it to overseas markets.
Q8. Do you have overseas cases, and how will you enter overseas markets?

A. We do not have specific overseas cases yet. But we have built a track record in Korea, and in particular we won a large public agency, the Korea Expressway Corporation, as a customer and delivered the system. As we expand abroad, we plan to present our domestic portfolio to overseas customers. We cannot go overseas directly, so we will work through overseas partners. If partners use our platform, they can apply it abroad right away, so we expect it to be a business that is easy to adopt.
Q9. What are your short-term plans?

A. In the short term, we aim to attend CES 2028. We also plan to take part in city-related exhibitions in Korea and abroad. Starting in 2027, we will use exhibitions to recruit partners for the platform we are completing this year.
Q10. What are the advantages of being based in Pangyo?

A. Pangyo has a high concentration of IT companies, so it offers a lot of support for IT firms. For a company like ours, demonstration on real roads is especially important. We ran the demonstration of CITY.AV communicating with the Panta-G Bus here in Pangyo, and the field demonstration of CITY.SIGNAL signal optimization here as well. Pangyo is IT-friendly and has many job seekers who want to work in IT, so it is also a very good place for an IT company to find new colleagues.
